title: Emergency authority over the Liquidity Layer is strictly subtractive: the Freezer can revoke a Relayer but never grant one
content:
A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.2 states the asymmetry precisely: "The Relayer Role may be granted to an address by any address holding the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`. The Relayer Role may be removed from an address by any address holding the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` **or the `FREEZER_ROLE`**." A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.4 confirms the Freezer's scope: "the emergency role that can remove a compromised Relayer."

The design principle is that an emergency power should be incapable of doing damage in the hands of an attacker. A compromised Freezer can halt Obex's allocation activity — disruptive, expensive, but recoverable. It cannot appoint a Relayer, mint, transfer, or redirect funds. The worst outcome of Freezer compromise is a denial of service; the worst outcome of admin compromise is loss of funds.

This is what justifies the Freezer's deliberately low bar elsewhere: a 2-of-5 multisig with mixed control (A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.1.2.2.3.2). Making a purely subtractive power easy to fire is cheap, because the cost of a false positive is bounded and the cost of hesitation in a real incident is not.

The corollary is that recovery is asymmetric too. Freezing takes two signatures from a five-key set; restoring a Relayer requires the admin, which is Sky Governance. Stopping is fast and unilateral; restarting is slow and constitutional — the correct ordering for a system holding other people's capital.
description: The Relayer Role may be granted only by DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, but removed by either DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE or FREEZER_ROLE — so emergency power can only reduce what the system is able to do.
